title: Headers, Content Negotiation & Compression
objectives: Classify HTTP headers into request, response, and entity families
Explain how Accept and Accept-Encoding drive content negotiation
Apply Vary and compression choices correctly behind caches and CDNs
body:
# Headers, Content Negotiation & Compression

## The problem
The same URL must serve browsers, mobile apps, CLI scripts, and crawlers. Some clients accept gzip, some brotli, some neither; some want JSON, others XML. HTTP solves this with a small set of general headers instead of per-client endpoints. Deciding which headers to honor - and which to ignore - is a core platform engineering skill.

## The header families
- General: `Cache-Control`, `Connection`, `Date`.
- Request: `Accept`, `Accept-Encoding`, `Authorization`, `Host`, `If-None-Match`.
- Response: `Content-Type`, `Content-Length`, `ETag`, `Vary`, `Content-Encoding`.
- Entity headers describe the body itself, independent of the transfer.

## Content negotiation
The server picks a representation from what the client offers:

```http
GET /api/users/42 HTTP/1.1
Accept: application/json
Accept-Encoding: gzip, br
```

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Encoding: br
Vary: Accept, Accept-Encoding
```

Preferences are expressed with quality values: `Accept: application/json;q=0.9, text/xml;q=0.5`. If the server cannot satisfy any offer it answers `406 Not Acceptable`, though many pragmatic APIs just default to JSON.

## Compression
- gzip: universal support, decent ratio, moderate CPU cost.
- brotli: better ratio, ideal for text and static assets, supported by all modern browsers over HTTPS.
- Never use `Content-Encoding` for data that is already compressed (images, video, zip): it wastes CPU and can even grow the payload.

## Vary: the header everyone forgets
If the response depends on a request header, caches must know: `Vary: Accept-Encoding` means a cached gzip copy must never be served to a client that cannot decode gzip. A missing `Vary` is how CDNs end up shipping corrupt representations.

## Decision framework
- Dynamic JSON at high CPU load? -> gzip at level 4-6; skip brotli quality 11.
- Static assets behind a CDN? -> precompress with brotli at build time.
- Proxy in the middle? -> make sure it does not strip `Accept-Encoding` and serve mismatched bodies.

## Best practices
- Send `Vary` for every request header that changes the representation.
- Set `Content-Type` with charset for text formats; browsers will guess otherwise.
- Precompress static assets; compress on the fly only for dynamic content.
- Reject unsupported request bodies with `415 Unsupported Media Type`.

## Common mistakes
- Compressing already-compressed payloads or payloads under ~1 KB.
- Forgetting `Vary: Accept-Encoding` behind a CDN, then shipping gzip bytes to a client that renders them as text.
- Reading `Accept: */*` as send-anything when it really means the client has no preference.
- Ignoring `Content-Length` / `Transfer-Encoding` when reading bodies, which breaks chunked uploads.

examples.name: curl-negotiate.sh
examples.code:
# Ask for JSON and let the server pick an encoding
curl -sD - -o /dev/null https://api.example.com/users/42 \
  -H "Accept: application/json" -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip, br"

# HTTP/1.1 200 OK
# Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
# Content-Encoding: br
# Vary: Accept, Accept-Encoding

exercise.prompt: Implement pickBest(header, supported): parse an Accept header with q-values and return the supported content type with the highest q. Honor the default q of 1 when absent, and let */* match any supported type. Return null when nothing matches.
hints: Split the header on commas, then split each entry on ; to separate the type from its parameters.
Default q is 1 when absent; sort offers by q descending before matching.
Match explicit types against the supported list first, then fall back to */*.

questions.prompt: A cache serves a gzip-encoded copy to a client that cannot decode gzip. Which missing response header caused this?
questions.explanation: Vary tells caches which request headers change the representation; without Accept-Encoding they reuse the wrong encoded copy for everyone.

questions.prompt: A client sends Accept: application/xml and the server only produces JSON. What is the most standard response?
questions.explanation: 406 signals the server cannot produce a representation matching Accept; 415 is for unsupported request bodies, not responses.

questions.prompt: Which payload should you NOT compress with Content-Encoding: gzip?
questions.explanation: Already-compressed data shrinks no further, wastes CPU, and can even grow; reserve Content-Encoding for text formats.
